who_it_covers: Any business that uses AI or automated tools to help make big decisions about people
what_it_requires: Post a clear notice before you use it. If someone gets a “no,” explain why within 30 days and let them fix wrong data and ask for a human review where that’s reasonable. Keep records 3 years.

who_it_covers: Anyone who builds or uses AI in Texas
what_it_requires: Don’t use AI meant to push people to self-harm or crime, to discriminate on purpose, to violate constitutional rights, or to make sexual deepfakes of kids. Health providers must tell patients about AI use.

who_it_covers: Businesses using generative AI with customers
what_it_requires: If a customer clearly asks whether they’re talking to AI, say so. Licensed professions (like health care or accounting) must say it up front in high-risk conversations.

who_it_covers: Any business using a chatbot with customers
what_it_requires: If a person could mistake your chatbot for a human, tell them clearly that it isn’t one.

who_it_covers: Employers using AI tools to hire, promote, discipline or fire
what_it_requires: Tell applicants and workers in plain language when they’re dealing with an AI hiring tool, and give written notice before the tool helps decide about them.
Don’t use AI that discriminates in hiring, promotion or firing, don’t use ZIP codes as a stand-in for race, and tell workers when you use AI for these decisions.
Don’t rely only on an automated decision system to discipline or fire a worker. If you mainly relied on one, a person has to review it. Give the worker a written notice afterward.
If a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is caused in whole or in large part by AI or other automated technology, say so in the notice and include details about the jobs and the system.

who_it_covers: Businesses and landlords using shared pricing software
what_it_requires: Don’t use pricing software fed with competitors’ data as part of a deal to fix prices.

who_it_covers: Businesses that price using a customer’s personal data
what_it_requires: Show “THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA.”
No rent-setting software that pools other landlords’ data.
No “revenue management” software fed with other landlords’ private data.

who_it_covers: Retail stores, food sellers, delivery apps; online sellers
what_it_requires: No surveillance pricing for stores and delivery apps; others must label it.

who_it_covers: Large food stores and delivery apps
what_it_requires: Can’t charge one shopper more for groceries using personal data.
No rent “coordinator” software or rent coordination.
No surveillance pricing; one-year pause on new electronic shelf labels.
If a listing photo was digitally altered (including with AI), say so and post the original online.

who_it_covers: Landlords and anyone listing a rental
what_it_requires: Same rule for rental listings.
If an ad prominently features an AI-made “synthetic performer,” disclose it clearly.
Disclose AI-made synthetic performers in ads. $1,000 first violation, $5,000 after.
AI can’t do therapy; admin use OK; consent to AI recording.
AI can’t deliver care directly; can’t market AI as a therapist.
Illinois-style limits.
Illinois-style limits plus consent to AI recording.
Illinois-style limits.
Breaking the AI rules is unprofessional conduct.
Can’t advertise AI as a mental health professional.

who_it_covers: Anyone offering a mental health chatbot
what_it_requires: Say it’s AI, label ads, don’t sell users’ health data.
AI can’t use titles that suggest a licensed health professional.
Label unreviewed AI-written patient messages and offer a way to reach a person.
Tell patients if AI documents the visit, and review the notes.
Use AI in diagnosis only within your license, review AI records, tell patients.
